title: Integrating Background Knowledge for Scalable Causal Discovery
claim: Skipping a test on a pair believed independent can wrongly create a collider, because the assumed empty separating set misleads orientation.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, red highlights marking the skipped edge and the wrongly oriented collider
description: Three small graph diagrams sit side by side, each with three circled nodes V, X and Y arranged as a triangle with V on top. The left panel, titled 'True DAG', shows black arrows X→V and V→Y and a red dashed line between X and Y. The middle panel, titled 'Skeleton', shows undirected black edges X–V and V–Y, a red dashed X–Y line, and a red 'Skip' label above the dashed line. The right panel, titled 'CPDAG', shows red arrows X→V and Y→V, which form a collider, with no X–Y edge. Beneath it, red text reads 'assume' and the formula sepset(X,Y)=∅ follows. Red marks the error. The eye goes first to the red dashed line and then to the red collider arrows.
caption: Skipping a CI test between $X$ and $Y$ due to a known gap $\mathcal{B} = X \gap Y$ and assuming that the separating set between $X$ and $Y$ is empty, leads to erroneously orienting an unshielded triple $X-V-Y$ as a v-structure in the CPDAG.
abstract: Expert background knowledge is often available in practical applications of causal discovery. Such constraints on the true causal graph can help causal discovery in terms of identifiability of causal effects and accuracy of the learned structure, but also in reducing the space of candidate causal graphs. As causal discovery can become computationally expensive for large number of variables, it is crucial to utilize background knowledge effectively during the causal discovery process. However, most current methods only use background knowledge in a postprocessing step after causal discovery to refine the learned graph. In this work, we develop a framework for utilizing background knowledge during the causal discovery process, focusing especially on scalable causal discovery methods that recover only a subset of the whole graph. We implement our framework for multiple algorithms and empirically show that utilizing background knowledge can both reduce computational requirements and increase the quality of the learned structures.
